title: Article I · Of the harm of evil thoughts

blocks.s: Every day we confess that we have sinned in thought; and yet who can shut and bridle his heart against thought? Indeed we sin more by affection than by thought; and yet by thought it happens that we sin in many ways and gravely. First, by dwelling on it too long. Hence through Jeremias God rebukes the man who thinks foolishly, saying: How long shall hurtful thoughts abide in thee? (Jer. iv, 14). Second, by a disordered and evil affection joined to the thought or born of it, as when someone, hearing, reading or meditating on stories of carnal things and doings, is touched by lust and unlawfully stirred, even at times in the divine Office and in holy places; which is wholly to be avoided. Third, on the side of time and of what does not belong there: as those who, at the time of divine things, and while they are free for better and more spiritual things and acts, are intent on temporal and outward things, for which they could lawfully be free at a fitting time. Which, alas, at the time of prayer and psalmody and celebration frequently befalls us. Fourth, on the side of the disorder and evil of the thoughts in themselves: as one who turns over and holds within himself vain imaginings and useless thoughts, which are not set under the order of divine love nor of use to it, such as melancholy apprehensions, bitter thoughts, rash judgements, unjust suspicions, immoderate searchings into high and incomprehensible things, fancies about things not to be thought of, and magnifyings of oneself. Of these and the like, and of the foolish boasting in them, the Lord speaks in the Prophets: Take away the evil of your devices from my eyes (Is. i, 16); and again: Woe to you that devise that which is unprofitable (Mich. ii, 1); and again: The Holy Spirit will withdraw himself from thoughts that are without understanding (Wisd. i, 5); perverse thoughts separate from God (Wisd. i, 3). In these things time is spent without fruit, and often lost in vice, and the mind itself is torn in itself, embittered and afflicted, according to the saying: A disordered mind is a punishment to itself. All such thoughts, therefore, are wholly to be avoided, quickly cast off, vehemently despised and hated.
